## The idea
Consider a second-order differential equation

$$\ddot{x}(t)=f(t,x(t),\dot{x}(t)).$$

Set $v(t)=\dot{x}(t)$. The equation becomes

$$\begin{cases}\dot{x}(t)=v(t),\\\dot{v}(t)=f(t,x(t),v(t)).\end{cases}$$

Position and velocity together form the **state** of the system. The initial data are $x(0)=x_0$ and $v(0)=v_0$.

## Example: the ideal pendulum
For a pendulum with no friction or external forcing, length $\ell>0$, and constant gravitational acceleration $g>0$,

$$\ddot{\theta}+\frac{g}{\ell}\sin\theta=0.$$

With $\omega=\dot{\theta}$, we obtain

$$\dot{\theta}=\omega,\qquad \dot{\omega}=-\frac{g}{\ell}\sin\theta.$$

Here $\theta$ is the angle measured from the downward vertical and $\omega$ is the angular velocity. The $(\theta,\omega)$ plane lets us study the system's trajectories.
